newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-COMPAGNONI AND WIBERG HOLD THE KEY.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-COMPAGNONI AND WIBERG HOLD THE KEY.

text.p: The rare sight of Pernilla Wiberg and Deborah Compagnoni in top form at the same time offers a compelling prospect for the women's races at the Alpine skiing world championships starting on Sunday.
Two of the most gifted skiers of the past decade, outspoken blonde Swede Wiberg and calm Italian brunette Compagnoni seem to have avoided one another for the past 10 years.
Injuries have helped make sure that the paths of the two 26-year-old racers did not cross.
When Wiberg became giant slalom world champion in 1991 in Saalbach, Compagnoni was just recovering from her fourth knee operation.

The Swede snatched Olympic gold in the discipline the next year on the very day when the Italian tore knee ligaments, returning to hospital once more. It took Compagnoni two years to reach her peak again.
Meanwhile, Wiberg in turn suffered a major setback, breaking her Achilles tendon in Maribor in 1993. The injury is still nagging her now.

Subsequently, Compagnoni took over the giant slalom supremacy, winning Olympic gold in Lillehammer in 1994 and a world crown last year at the world championships in Sierra Nevada, where Wiberg took the slalom and combined titles.
For the first time, they will both be at their best in Sestriere, having each won four World Cup races this season.
Even then they seem to have avoided one another in a way, Wiberg shining mostly in slalom and super-G while Compagnoni won three giant slaloms.
As if to underline their differences, Compagnoni has suggested she may not race the super-G in Sestriere while Wiberg hinted she would like to win downhill and super-G medals to complete her set.
The Swede, currently leading the World Cup, has reasons to believe in her chances in the downhill, which has never been her favourite event in the past and which she has never won.
In 1994, she blew her chance of snatching the overall World Cup title when she crashed in a downhill in Vail.
This season, another injury, similar to the one her American friend Picabo Street has been nursing since the start of the winter campaign, leaves the race wide open.
The world champion has given some advice to Wiberg, who now stands along with the best specialists in downhills.
With last season's World Cup winner Katja Seizinger suffering from lack of confidence, the long delayed showdown between Wiberg and Compagnoni may well take place at last.
The pair may be challenged by Italy's super-G champion Isolde Kostner or her compatriot and giant specialist Sabina Panzanini.
Panzanini, however, does have something of a question mark over her, having injured her Achilles earlier in the month.
